notes.meaning: God calls His people to pay attention and reminds them that they are His chosen servants. Even after warning them of judgment for their sins, He assures them of His ongoing favor. They belong to the Lord and are not abandoned.

God reminds Israel that He made them and formed them into a people from the very beginning. He calls them Jeshurun, a special title meaning upright one, showing His tender grace toward a flawed nation. Because the Lord pledges to help them, they do not need to live in fear.

The Lord promises to pour water on parched ground, using rain as a picture of giving His Holy Spirit. This promised outpouring would refresh weary souls and bring spiritual life to their children. God brings renewal and fruitfulness wherever His Spirit moves.
Under the blessing of the Holy Spirit, the people and their children will thrive and grow. They are compared to green willows shooting up rapidly along fresh, flowing streams.

People will step forward gladly to declare that they belong to the Lord. Some will write God's name on their hands to show lifelong devotion, like a loyal servant dedicated to a master. This also looks ahead to people from other nations joining God's family.

The Lord introduces Himself as Israel's King and Redeemer, the one who rescues and protects them. He announces that He is the first and the last, having no beginning and no end. Beside Him, no other true God exists.
The Lord challenges any false god to match what He has done. Only the true God has guided history from ancient times and accurately foretold what will happen in the days to come.

God tells His people to stop trembling in fear. He had already revealed the future long before it happened, and His people are living witnesses of His faithfulness. He is the only dependable Rock who can keep them safe.

People who make idols are pursuing total emptiness, and their treasured statues have no real power to help. The idols can neither see nor understand anything, which leaves their makers disgraced in the end.
The prophet exposes the senseless act of trying to manufacture a god. A carved or cast metal statue is completely useless and can do nothing for the person who made it.

All the workers and craftsmen who join together to make idols will be put to shame. They are merely mortal men, and frail humans cannot create the divine. Standing before God, their false work leaves them terrified and confused.

A blacksmith works hard over glowing coals, hammering iron into tools to carve an image. He labors so fiercely that he grows hungry, thirsty, and tired. The very god he is helping to produce cannot even keep him from growing faint.
A carpenter measures wood, outlines a figure with chalk, and carves it with tools into human form. He makes it look like an attractive person just so it can sit motionless inside a shrine or house.

A man cuts down cedar, cypress, or oak trees from the forest to get his materials. He might even plant a tree himself, but it still relies on the rain God sends in order to grow. The very wood used for the idol is something God provided.

A single tree ends up serving two completely different purposes for the same person. He burns some of the wood to warm his home and bake bread, but then takes another piece of that same log, carves a god out of it, and bows down to worship it.
The craftsman burns half the log in a fire to cook his meat and enjoy a hot meal. He sits comfortably by the blaze, delighted by the warmth and cheering flames.
From whatever leftover wood remains, the man carves a statue and calls it his god. He falls on his knees before the block of wood, begging it to save him and protect his life.

Idol worshipers lack understanding because their spiritual eyes and hearts are closed to reality. Because they stubbornly chose worthless images, God gave them over to the blindness of their own foolish minds.

The idol worshiper never stops to think carefully about what he is doing. He fails to realize the obvious contradiction of burning half a log for cooking and then bowing down to worship the rest of the stick.

Trusting in an idol is as empty and useless as trying to satisfy real hunger by eating ashes. A deceived heart leads the person astray, keeping him from seeing that the god in his hand is a complete lie.
God urges Israel to take these lessons to heart and avoid the foolish trap of idols. They are His special servants whom He created, and He reassures them that He will never forget them.

The Lord promises to wipe away Israel's sins completely, just like the morning sun scatters heavy clouds and mist. Because He has purchased their freedom, He lovingly invites them to turn back to Him.

All creation is invited to burst into songs of praise, from the highest heavens to the lowest depths and mountain forests. Nature celebrates because the Lord has redeemed His people and shown His glory through them.
The Lord reveals Himself as Israel's Redeemer who formed them from the womb. He alone created the entire universe, stretching out the skies and spreading out the earth without any partner.
God exposes the false signs of pagan fortune-tellers and shows that their omens are empty lies. He frustrates worldly counselors and turns their supposed wisdom into foolish nonsense.

While false predictions collapse, the Lord faithfully fulfills every word spoken by His true prophets. He promises that ruined Jerusalem will be lived in once more and that Judah's broken towns will be rebuilt.

The Lord shows His sovereign power by commanding deep ocean currents and rivers to dry up. This reminds Israel of how God opened the Red Sea and points ahead to Babylon's river defenses being dried up when the city falls.

The Lord names Cyrus long before his birth, calling this Persian king His shepherd to carry out His divine plan. Through Cyrus, God would ensure that Jerusalem was rebuilt and the temple's foundations laid once again.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars believe these verses were written during or after the Babylonian exile by a later writer, rather than by Isaiah foretelling Cyrus by name centuries before his birth.
